performers: Sviatoslav Richter, Warsaw National Philharmonic Orchestra, Stanisław Wisłocki
intro: In the Adagio sostenuto of the Piano Concerto No. 2, Op. 18, a flute begins the long melody and a clarinet continues it, while Sviatoslav Richter plays arpeggios on the piano beneath them. A stormy middle section comes before the movement returns to E major.

sections.label: Intro · Muted strings modulate to E major
sections.mNote: Four slow bars modulate from C minor

sections.label: A · Flute and clarinet over piano
sections.mNote: A long wind melody above repeated piano arpeggios

sections.label: B · Short phrases over piano semiquavers
sections.mNote: The winds alternate with the piano in brief phrases.

sections.label: Cadenza · Solo piano cadenza
sections.mNote: Orchestral chords alternate with solo piano runs

sections.label: A′ · Slow theme in E major
sections.mNote: E major arpeggios accompany the violin melody as it returns.

sections.label: A″ · Piano chords with wind replies
sections.mNote: The piano plays the melody above broken chords; flutes play staccato.

sections.label: Coda · The last E major chords
sections.mNote: Wind phrases fall silent above the sustained strings

relations.label: The slow melody returns
relations.basis: The outer E-major song returns after the quicker middle and cadenza. These long excerpts compare its continuation in A and A′, with the later span inside the return marked near 524 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.952, sustained 71 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 495 s (cache/form/rachmaninoff-concerto-2-adagio.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Introduction, C minor to E major
cues.text: Muted strings begin in C minor, the key of the first movement. Clarinets, bassoons and horns join their slow chords as the notes move by semitones. The four-bar introduction modulates to E major, where the piano enters with arpeggios.
cues.evidence: Gutheil full score, Boosey & Hawkes reprint, p. 48: four-bar introduction, muted strings, wind entries and E major piano entrance. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP528309-PMLP01953-Rachmaninoff_-_Piano_Concerto_No._2_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Flute and clarinet solos
cues.text: The flute plays the melody above arpeggiated figures in the piano. A clarinet continues the phrase, marked dolce e sempre espressivo (sweetly, always expressive), while the piano accompaniment continues underneath.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 48–49, rehearsal 17: arpeggiated piano accompaniment, flute solo and clarinet continuation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Partial première, Moscow, 1900
cues.text: On 15 December 1900, in Moscow, Rachmaninoff played the Adagio and finale with Alexander Siloti conducting, at a concert for the Ladies’ Charity Prison Committee. The audience received the music enthusiastically. He had not yet finished the first movement.
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel’s BSO note gives the date, performers, charity, reception and order of completion. https://www.bso.org/works/piano-concerto-no-2-6

cues.title: Piano figuration with wind replies
cues.text: From rehearsal 20 the piano plays quick figures. Bassoons and horns reply in short phrases, and the bass line in the lower strings moves beneath the repeated shapes. The long opening melody is divided into shorter exchanges between soloist and orchestra.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 53–56, from rehearsal 20: moving piano figures, bassoon and horn answers, changing lower-string bass.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Piano cadenza, rehearsal 25
cues.text: The orchestra holds a chord and the piano continues alone. Runs climb through the keyboard, broken off by thick chords, and trills follow. The Adagio sostenuto then returns.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 62–64, rehearsal 25 and cadenza: held orchestral chord, solo runs, chords, trills and return to Adagio sostenuto.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the opening theme, violins
cues.text: Adagio sostenuto, Tempo I. The piano returns to E major arpeggios, and the first violins take up the opening melody, marked espressivo.
cues.evidence: Full score, p. 64: Adagio sostenuto, Tempo I, pp piano arpeggios and first-violin melody marked p espressivo.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Nikolai Dahl, dedicatee
cues.text: Nikolai Dahl, the doctor to whom Rachmaninoff dedicated the concerto, was an amateur musician who hosted chamber-music evenings. In 1900 the composer visited him daily for treatment. The dedication “À Monsieur N. Dahl” stands above the opening bars on the concerto’s first page.
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel’s BSO note documents Dahl’s musical interests and the daily treatment in January–April 1900. The dedication appears on p. 3 of the full score. https://www.bso.org/works/piano-concerto-no-2-6

cues.title: Piano melody with staccato flutes
cues.text: At rehearsal 27 the piano plays the melody in chords over an arpeggiated left hand. Above it, the flutes play short staccato figures and the strings hold sustained notes.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 66–67, rehearsal 27: chordal piano melody, arpeggiated left hand, staccato flute figures and sustained strings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final bars, E major chord
cues.text: The wind phrases stop, and the piano’s last moving notes sound above sustained strings. A final upward figure reaches the E major chord, which piano and strings hold together under a fermata.
cues.evidence: Full score, p. 67, final system: withdrawing winds, final piano figure and E major chord held with the strings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Muted string chords to piano entry
transitions.from: Intro · Muted strings modulate to E major
transitions.to: A · Flute and clarinet over piano
transitions.how: The muted strings play chords in C minor that move chromatically into E major. The piano enters at p with broken chords that circle over a low E. A solo flute begins the melody and a clarinet continues it, while the piano keeps up its steady motion beneath.
transitions.evidence: Gutheil full score, Boosey & Hawkes reprint, pp. 48–49, introduction and rehearsal 17.

transitions.title: Wind phrases around the piano
transitions.from: A · Flute and clarinet over piano
transitions.to: B · Short phrases over piano semiquavers
transitions.how: The piano’s quick notes move out of the background. Its hands exchange short phrases, and bassoons, horns and upper winds reply with short phrases of their own. Beneath the repeated figures the lower strings move the harmony through chromatic changes away from the E major of the opening.
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 53–56, from rehearsal 20: piano figures, short wind phrases and moving bass.

transitions.title: Orchestral chord and fermata before the cadenza
transitions.from: B · Short phrases over piano semiquavers
transitions.how: Beneath the piano’s rising run, the timpani roll and the wind, trombones and strings hold sustained notes in a crescendo. At rehearsal 25 the orchestra plays a chord, followed by a long fermata over rests. The piano then continues alone, climbing from the bass in runs and trills.
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 62–64: timpani roll, held orchestral harmony, rehearsal 25 and the solo cadenza.

transitions.title: Cadenza to Tempo I
transitions.to: A′ · Slow theme in E major
transitions.how: The piano’s long run ends in a trill and a ritardando. At Adagio sostenuto, Tempo I the E major arpeggios return at pp. The first violins play the melody again, p espressivo, above the low E and the soloist’s circling notes.
transitions.evidence: Full score, p. 64: end of the cadenza, Tempo I, E major piano accompaniment and returning violin melody.

transitions.title: Winds drop out before the final chord
transitions.from: A″ · Piano chords with wind replies
transitions.to: Coda · The last E major chords
transitions.how: The flutes and clarinets finish their short figures and stop. The strings hold their notes while the piano completes its broken chords and final rising line. The harmony stays in E major under the closing phrase, and piano and strings end together under a fermata.
transitions.evidence: Full score, p. 67, closing systems: wind rests, sustained strings and final E major chord.

source.title: Rachmaninoff, Piano Concerto No. 2, II. Adagio sostenuto, full score (Gutheil; Boosey & Hawkes reprint)
source.locator: Printed pp. 48–67, rehearsal figures 17–27: muted-string introduction, wind melody, cadenza and E major return. Two trombones and timpani join the approach to the cadenza on p. 62.

timeline.note: Muted strings move from C minor towards E major; clarinets, bassoons and horns join the slow chords.
The flute begins the melody and the clarinet continues it over arpeggios in the piano.
The piano takes up the melody, with woodwind replies and divided strings beneath it.
A bassoon answers the piano’s phrases over quiet strings.
The piano’s quick figures are answered briefly by bassoons, clarinets and horns.
Upper winds exchange short phrases above piano arpeggios and the lower-string bass.
Winds, horns and strings hold long notes around the piano’s increasingly forceful figures.
Two trombones and a timpani roll join the orchestral crescendo before the piano’s cadenza.
The piano climbs through runs and trills, interrupted by full chords and pauses.
First violins return to the opening melody above the piano’s quiet E major arpeggios.
Piano and strings carry the broad line beneath short staccato flute and clarinet figures.
The wind phrases end; the piano continues in broken chords above sustained strings.
The piano completes its last rising figure, and the strings hold the final E major chord with it.

composer.epithet: Russian composer and pianist who earned his living at the piano in exile and whose music uses the sound of the bells of his childhood.
facts: Zverev and Siloti at the piano; Taneyev and Arensky in composition
Ivanovka, Dresden, New York, Villa Senar and Beverly Hills
Four piano concertos, three symphonies, three completed operas, choral music, songs and piano works

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Rachmaninoff to Leonard Liebling, 1939; published in The Musical Courier, 5 April 1943

composer.background:
“My hearty thanks to the old man for not having forgotten about me!” Rachmaninoff wrote to the singer Mikhail Slonov on 26 December 1892. The old man was Tchaikovsky, who had praised his opera Aleko in a newspaper interview. Rachmaninoff was nineteen and had recently graduated from the Moscow Conservatory with its Great Gold Medal. Tchaikovsky helped get the opera into the Bolshoi, and in May 1893 he sat in the audience and applauded.

His childhood had been less settled. He was born into a landowning family and grew up at Oneg, near Novgorod, until his father’s financial failures forced a move to St Petersburg. He entered the Conservatory there in 1883. His parents separated, his sister Sofia died of diphtheria, and his schoolwork went badly. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where he heard the choirs and bells he remembered all his life. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended that he move to Moscow to study with the piano teacher Nikolai Zverev, who was known for his strictness.
